frameworks.name: Four Buyer Screening Criteria
frameworks.definition: Four non-negotiable attributes of a market before entry: audience is in pain, easy to identify, has money to spend, and the market is growing.

frameworks.name: Marketing Method-Platform-Media-Volume Hierarchy
frameworks.definition: Four-layer decomposition of customer acquisition: method (paid ads, content, outreach, affiliates), platform (Facebook, email, YouTube, Google), media type within platform (stories, posts, reels, DMs), and volume executed within media.

frameworks.name: Pyramid of Markets Expansion
frameworks.definition: Five directional vectors for market expansion: up-market (fewer, higher-spend customers), down-market (more volume customers), adjacent (similar business characteristics), broader (entire psychographic), or narrower (hyper-specific niches).

claims.text: When an entrepreneur hits their first plateau in customer acquisition, they typically assume the market is saturated and initiate new product lines or business diversification. However, the real constraint is not market saturation but mindset saturation—they have not exhausted the method, platform, media, or volume levers available within their current niche.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: entrepreneur with profitable core business ($1M+ profit, $3M+ top-line revenue)
showing growth plateau despite significant ad spend ($50k/month)
considering expansion into new product lines or niches
claims.mechanism: The operator confuses market cap (total addressable audience) with personal capacity utilization. They have tapped one channel deeply but not tested methodological, platform, media-type, or volume variations.
bounded_by: Applies to service and productized businesses with defined customer avatars
Does not apply when the operator has demonstrably saturated all method-platform-media-volume combinations within their niche
Does not apply when the niche is genuinely small (e.g., <10,000 addressable customers globally)

claims.text: For a given customer avatar and market, there are exactly four acquisition levers that can be turned before market saturation is real: the method (the how: paid ads, content, outreach, referrals, affiliates); the platform (where: Facebook, email, YouTube, Google); the media within that platform (Instagram DMs vs. posts vs. stories vs. reels); and the volume executed in each media (1 story/week vs. multiple stories/day).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: single avatar, single niche, pre-saturation stage
claims.mechanism: Each lever multiplies available reach: more methods × more platforms × more media variations × more volume = geometric expansion of addressable lead volume without changing the core offer.

numbers.axis: acquisition lever count before market saturation claimed

anchors.value: market saturation true, niche pivot justified

bounded_by: Assumes the core offer is profitable and scalable
Does not include offer redesign or audience narrowing (separate levers)

claims.text: When selecting an initial market or evaluating whether to pivot, evaluate based on four mandatory criteria: (1) Are the prospects in acute pain? (2) Are they easy to find? (3) Do they have the money to spend? (4) Is the market growing? If a market fails any of these, it is not worth entering.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: market selection decision (initial entry or pivot)
before significant capital or time deployment
claims.mechanism: A market failing on any single criterion introduces one of four fatal flaws: low motivation (no pain), high sales-cost (hard to find), no budget (can't afford), or market death (no growth velocity). Any single flaw is sufficient to render the market economically unviable at scale.
bounded_by: Criterion #4 (market growth) is especially important because a stagnant niche caps absolute revenue even if the first three criteria are met

claims.text: At scale, there is a finite volume of addressable customers you can reach within a single niche (e.g., 50,000 microgyms in the United States); after exhausting all method-platform-media-volume combinations, the market reaches true saturation and expansion into adjacent or parallel markets becomes necessary, not optional.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: market-leading position within a niche
all four levers (method, platform, media, volume) are maxed out
direct-response channels exhausted (ads, cold email, cold calls, content)
claims.mechanism: Total addressable market (TAM) is finite. When you have contacted/exposed your offer to ~40% of the TAM and are running saturated campaigns across all channels, growth velocity from the existing niche floor.

numbers.axis: market penetration in an example niche

bounded_by: Does not apply if the operator has not maximized method, platform, media, and volume across all channels

claims.text: When expanding from a saturated niche into adjacent or parallel markets, rank expansion candidates by the total dollar value of results you can deliver to each avatar. The highest-dollar-impact avatar (up-market if enterprise; down-market if volume; adjacent if similar economics) should be attacked first, even if it requires a different sales motion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: market leader in existing niche
genuine TAM saturation confirmed
multiple adjacent markets available
claims.mechanism: Maximizing dollar value per customer (LTV) and cost to acquire (CAC) ratio across avatar options reveals the highest-return expansion path. An avatar with smaller total addressable numbers but 10x higher per-customer value can yield more absolute revenue than a high-volume down-market expansion.
bounded_by: Assumes your core competency (core offer value delivery) transfers materially across the avatar boundaries
Does not apply if customer acquisition motion is fundamentally different (e.g., enterprise vs. self-serve)

claims.text: The Pyramid of Markets defines five mutually exclusive expansion directions from any niche: (1) up-market (enterprise, larger players, higher spend, fewer total addressable customers); (2) down-market (individual contributors, higher volume, lower spend); (3) adjacent markets (similar business model, similar avatar profile, different industry or specific outcome); (4) broader umbrella (entire psychographic category); (5) narrower specialization (hyper-specific sub-niche). At most, an operator can pursue 1-2 directions simultaneously without diluting focus.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: post-saturation expansion decision
market-leading position in core niche proven
claims.mechanism: Each direction requires distinct messaging, offer positioning, and sometimes sales motion. Attempting simultaneous expansion across 3+ directions introduces operational chaos and kills unit economics on each.

anchors.value: fewer total addressable, higher CAC, higher LTV
10x higher volume, lower LTV, different sales motion
similar owner psychographic, similar business model

anchors.region: broader: all beauty professionals (med spa, massage, etc.)
anchors.value: expand TAM 5-10x at cost of messaging precision loss

bounded_by: A narrower specialization (direction #5) is the only direction that does NOT increase TAM but may increase per-customer revenue if offer specificity and value delivery improve dramatically

claims.text: Niche-down (narrower specialization) can yield 2-5x revenue growth despite cutting addressable market by 85%, if the specific sub-niche avatar perceives 10x higher value from your specialized offering relative to the broad-market offer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: existing business with 100% broad-market positioning
sub-segment (15% of current market) perceives disproportionate value
sub-segment willing to pay premium for specialized outcome
claims.mechanism: Specialization allows extreme offer optimization and messaging clarity; the 15% of customers who remain generate 2-5x prior revenue because of price premium and reduced CAC from precision targeting.

anchors.value: 200-500% of baseline revenue from 15% of original market

bounded_by: Requires the narrower sub-segment to genuinely perceive 10x higher value (not just 2x or 3x)
Only applicable if the sub-niche is still large enough to support the operator's growth goals (not <1000 customers globally)

claims.text: Businesses that plateau at first growth ceiling often have not explored all method, platform, media, and volume options within their current niche, yet immediately pursue new product lines or new markets. This adds operational complexity without addressing the root cause: the founder has failed to scale the existing business model within the existing market.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: post-first-plateau stage (typically $1M-$3M revenue)
multiple methods/platforms/media available but untested
founder contemplating new product lines or markets
claims.mechanism: New products and new markets introduce new unit economics, new sales motions, and new operational systems. These multiply complexity faster than they multiply revenue. The operator regresses on all dimensions while learning the new business model.
bounded_by: Does not apply once all four acquisition levers are genuinely maxed out within the core niche and the market size is confirmed to be <$10M addressable annual revenue

claims.text: At an 8-person CEO cohort with combined $500M revenue (averaging $62.5M per CEO), the two distinguishing factors between Alex Hormozi (~$30M at that time) and the higher-earning founders were: (1) Most had been in business longer (supporting the thesis that major business outcomes require 5-10+ years). (2) They were pursuing larger markets and/or higher-value customers than Hormozi was.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: high-performing founder cohort (>$20M annual revenue each)
similar market conditions and access
comparable skill levels and work ethic
claims.mechanism: Time-in-market compounds non-linearly: systems improve, brand strengthens, team builds, market repeats emerge. Larger markets (more total addressable customers) limit ceiling regardless of operator skill.

numbers.axis: Hormozi cohort revenue and time-in-business correlation

anchors.value: ~$62.5M annual revenue (2x Hormozi at that point)
longer-tenured peers averaging 5-10+ more years of business operation

bounded_by: Assumes similar market selection criteria are met for all founders (pain, findability, budget, growth)
Does not account for acqui-hire dynamics or capital deployment that can accelerate peers' growth

claims.text: Many entrepreneurs assume their market is capped when they hit the ceiling of one acquisition channel (e.g., $50k/month in Facebook ad spend with diminishing returns). In reality, the market is not capped; their mindset and channel focus is capped. An industry with $60 billion in annual revenue and the operator capturing <1% has vast headroom before true saturation occurs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: operator has hit ceiling on single acquisition channel
total addressable market is significantly larger than current revenue
operator is contemplating new products/niches prematurely
claims.mechanism: A single channel (Facebook ads, cold email, affiliates) can saturate for technical or economic reasons (ad cost inflation, email fatigue, partner concentration), but the broader market remains untapped. Other methods, platforms, and media segments are available.

anchors.value: operator at <1% of total industry addressable revenue

bounded_by: Applies only when TAM is >$10M annually
Does not apply to true niche markets with <$50M TAM where single-channel saturation signals genuine market cap

examples.text: Gym Launch pivoted from targeting only microgyms (50,000 total in the USA, with Gym Launch having contacted ~20,000 of them) to also targeting health clubs. This expansion was driven by the insight that health club owners derived 10x higher dollar value from Gym Launch's restructuring of onboarding, sales, retention, and upsell processes compared to microgym owners. Despite the TAM being smaller in absolute numbers, the higher per-customer value made health clubs a more attractive expansion vector than moving down-market to personal trainers.

A salon owner applying an up-market expansion would pursue franchisors or multi-location chain operators instead of individual salon owners. A down-market expansion would pursue individual hairstylists renting chairs (10x higher volume but lower revenue per customer). An adjacent expansion might target lash-and-nails studios with similar owner profiles and business models. A broader expansion would encompass the entire beauty industry (med spa owners, massage studios, lash owners), increasing TAM 5-10x but reducing messaging precision. A narrower specialization might focus exclusively on Brazilian-blowout specialists, potentially increasing revenue 2-5x from a 15% reduced addressable market.

A chiropractor agency market has ~100 competing agencies, all marketing to chiropractors on Facebook. Adding up all of their combined ad spend across Facebook reveals the total pool of new chiropractor leads available monthly from that single channel. If a single agency wants to grow leads beyond that pool's saturation, it must either (1) outbid competitors on Facebook (unlikely to improve margins), or (2) expand to other methods (cold email, phone outreach, partnerships), other platforms (Google, YouTube, LinkedIn), other media on existing platforms (content, webinars, referral programs), or increase volume (more posts, more outreach calls).

practices.text: Exhaust all four acquisition levers (method, platform, media, volume) within your current niche and market before expanding to new product lines or new markets. If you believe you are hitting a growth ceiling, perform an audit: (1) how many of the five methods (paid ads, content, outreach, referrals, affiliates) are you running? (2) how many platforms per method are you on? (3) how many media types within each platform? (4) what is your current volume on each media (posts/day, calls/day, email/week)? Address this checklist before expanding.

Before entering or pivoting to a new market, validate all four buyer-screening criteria: (1) Are prospects in acute pain or solving a critical problem? (2) Are they easy to identify and reach? (3) Do they have sufficient budget to pay for a premium solution? (4) Is the market growing (not stagnant or declining)? If any criterion fails, the market is not worth pursuing.

When expanding from a saturated niche, rank your options by the dollar value you can deliver to each avatar. Test and measure revenue impact per customer across up-market, down-market, adjacent, and broader expansion directions. Double down on the direction that yields the highest unit economics, not the direction with the largest absolute market size.

If you are considering niche-down specialization (narrowing your addressable market by 70-85% to hyper-specialize), quantify the value-perception uplift in the narrower segment. You should only niche down if the specialized sub-segment perceives 8-10x higher value from your offer (measured by price premium, reduced close cycle, improved retention) compared to your broad-market offering.

Accept that building significant business scale is a multi-year endeavor (5-10+ years is typical for market-leading exits). Avoid the trap of constantly pivoting to new markets or new products because the current trajectory feels slow. Instead, invest in market-leading status within a single niche before expanding.
